title: Joint injection
what: The doctor injects medicine right into the joint with a thin needle. Sometimes extra fluid is drained from the joint first.
why: For joint pain and inflammation, for arthritis when tablets and other treatment do not help much, and to test fluid from the joint.
tell_doctor: Diabetes. Some medicines raise blood sugar
If you have a fever, a cold, or a skin sore near the joint
How many injections you had in this joint before

prepare.title: Preparation
prepare.text: Usually nothing special is needed. You can eat as usual.

prepare.title: Medicines
prepare.text: Do not stop your medicines. If you take blood thinners, tell your doctor. They will decide.

prepare.title: Clothes
prepare.text: Loose clothes, so the joint is easy to uncover.

prepare.title: Getting home
prepare.text: If the injection is in the knee or hip, it is best to have someone drive you home.

bring: X-rays and reports about the joint
steps: You lie or sit so the joint is easy to reach
The doctor finds the injection spot, sometimes with ultrasound
The skin is carefully cleaned with antiseptic
Sometimes the skin is numbed first
The doctor puts the needle into the joint and drains fluid, if needed
The medicine is injected, the needle is removed, and a plaster is put on
feel: A prick and a feeling of pressure in the joint
If fluid is drained, the feeling of fullness goes away
after: Usually rest the joint for 1 to 2 days: no heavy activity or long walks
Sometimes pain gets worse in the first 24 hours. Cold helps
You can take off the plaster after a few hours
The effect often starts after a few days
If you have diabetes, check your blood sugar more often in the next few days
red_flags: The joint becomes hot, red, very swollen, or the pain gets worse: see a doctor right away
A fever above 38 degrees in the first days after the injection

faq.a: When everything is kept clean, the risk is small. The main thing is to tell your doctor right away if the joint turns red and hot.

faq.q: How many times can a joint be injected?
faq.a: It depends on the medicine. Steroids are usually not injected often. Your doctor will tell you how many you can have.
